source: A changing magnetic flux makes an emf: ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt.
Students think a strong but steady field makes an emf, when only a changing flux does.

In Generators and Induction you saw that moving a magnet near a coil makes a current. Faraday found the rule behind it in 1831, and it runs every generator and transformer. It is stated in terms of Magnetic Flux.

A changing magnetic flux through a coil of $N$ turns makes an emf $$\role[emf]{voltage}{\varepsilon} = -\role[number of turns]{constant}{N}\frac{\role[change in magnetic flux]{field}{\Delta\Phi}}{\role[time interval]{time}{\Delta t}}.$$ The size is $N|\Delta\Phi|/\Delta t$. The minus sign is Lenz's law, which sets the direction (the next topic). A steady flux, however large, makes no emf.
The meter swings only while the flux changes. With the magnet resting inside the coil, the flux is large but steady, and the emf is zero.

Why the rate of change? An emf is energy per charge. Pushing a magnet in faster does the same change in less time, so the same work is done more quickly on the charges: a bigger emf for a shorter time. The emf times the time, $\varepsilon\,\Delta t = -N\Delta\Phi$, depends only on how much the flux changed.

Thinking a strong but steady field makes an emf. A magnet sitting still inside a coil makes no current at all. Only a change in flux counts. Check: if nothing in $\Phi = BA\cos\theta$ is changing, the answer is $0\ \text{V}$.
A coil of $200$ turns with area $0.010\ \text{m}^2$ faces a field that grows from $0.10\ \text{T}$ to $0.50\ \text{T}$ in $0.20\ \text{s}$. Find the emf.
Change in flux per turn: $$\Delta\Phi = \Delta B \cdot A = (0.40)(0.010) = 4.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{Wb}.$$
A single loop of area $0.20\ \text{m}^2$ faces a $0.30\ \text{T}$ field. It is turned edge-on in $0.15\ \text{s}$. The loop has a resistance of $2.0\ \Omega$. Find the average emf and current.
